title: What is Java?
tagline: The language that runs on 3 billion devices
analogy: Java is like a movie streaming service: you write your movie once (source code), the studio converts it to a universal format (bytecode), and then every device with the 'player app' (the JVM) can watch it — no matter what brand the device is.
content: Java was created by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems in 1995. Today it powers Android apps, banking systems, Netflix, Amazon, and most enterprise backends.

The three core pieces are the JDK (Java Development Kit — compiler + tools), the JRE (Java Runtime Environment — libraries + JVM), and the JVM (Java Virtual Machine — the engine that executes bytecode).
Java is compiled to bytecode (.class files), not machine code. Bytecode is a platform-neutral intermediate language that any JVM can execute.
This 'compile once, run anywhere' (WORA) model is what makes Java portable across Windows, Linux, macOS, mainframes, and embedded devices.
Java is statically typed: every variable's type is known at compile time, which catches many bugs before your program even runs.
Memory is managed automatically by the garbage collector — you create objects and the JVM reclaims them when they are no longer reachable.
The Java ecosystem includes the standard library (java.* packages), build tools (Maven, Gradle), and huge frameworks (Spring, Hibernate) for real-world applications.
Java releases on a 6-month cadence today, with long-term support (LTS) versions like Java 8, 11, 17, and 21 that enterprises actually run in production.
commonMistakes: Confusing JDK, JRE, and JVM — remember JDK contains the compiler, the JVM is the runtime engine.
Believing Java compiles directly to machine code — it compiles to bytecode first.
Forgetting that you need a JDK (not just a JRE) to compile with javac.

title: Hello, World! — Your First Program
tagline: Anatomy of a Java program, dissected
analogy: A Java file is like a recipe card: the class is the recipe book's title, the main method is the 'start here' instruction, and each statement is a step that runs top to bottom.
content: Every Java program lives inside a class. The file name must match the public class name: Main.java contains public class Main.
The main method is the JVM's entry point — it must be exactly: public static void main(String[] args).
public means the JVM can access it from outside the class; static means it exists without creating an object; void means it returns nothing.
The args parameter receives command-line arguments as an array of Strings.
System.out.println() prints a line to the console; System.out.print() prints without a newline.
Statements end with a semicolon ; and blocks are delimited by curly braces {}.
Compile with javac Main.java to produce Main.class, then run with java Main.
The code block defines the scope: anything declared inside {} is only visible inside that block.
commonMistakes: Naming the file differently from the public class — javac will refuse or run the wrong class.
Writing main as main(String[] args) without public static void.
Forgetting the semicolon after statements.
Running java HelloWorld.class instead of java HelloWorld.

title: Variables and Data Types
tagline: Java's typed boxes for storing data
analogy: Think of variables as labeled boxes in a warehouse. Each box type has a fixed size: an int box holds small whole numbers, a long box holds big ones, a double box holds decimals with a decimal point, and a boolean box holds just true or false. You cannot stuff a giraffe (String) into a mouse-sized int box.
content: Java has 8 primitive types: byte (8-bit), short (16-bit), int (32-bit), long (64-bit), float (32-bit), double (64-bit), char (16-bit Unicode), and boolean.
Reference types live on the heap and are accessed through references: String, arrays, and your own classes. A reference stores the memory address of an object, not the object itself.
Primitives are passed by value; references are also passed by value (the reference is copied, so the object is shared).
Choose the right type: use int for most counting, long for large values, double for decimals, boolean for flags.
Type conversion: widening (int to long) is automatic and safe; narrowing (long to int) requires an explicit cast and may lose data.
Integer overflow silently wraps: Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 becomes Integer.MIN_VALUE. Watch for it in calculations.
char stores a single 16-bit Unicode character; use String for text of any length.
Local variables must be initialized before use — the compiler enforces this with 'variable might not have been initialized'.
commonMistakes: Using int for values that exceed ~2.1 billion — use long and append L.
Using double for money — floating point cannot represent decimal fractions exactly; use BigDecimal.
Forgetting that 7 / 2 is 3, not 3.5, because both operands are integers.
Assuming assigning a new value to one reference variable mutates the other — references copy the address, not the object.

title: Operators
analogy: Operators are like the buttons on a calculator with a brain: + - * / do arithmetic, == and > compare two values like a referee, && and || combine true/false flags like a bouncer checking both ID and ticket.
content: Arithmetic: + - * / and % (modulo). Integer division truncates; to get decimals, one operand must be floating point.
Modulo % gives the remainder: 7 % 3 is 1. It is perfect for cycling, parity checks, and digit extraction.
Comparison operators: ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= return a boolean result.
Logical operators: && (AND), || (OR), ! (NOT). Short-circuiting means && stops if the left side is false, and || stops if the left side is true.
Assignment operators: =, +=, -=, *=, /=, %=. They are shorthand for modifying a variable.
Increment/decrement: ++ and -- with prefix (++i increments first) and postfix (i++ evaluates first) semantics.
Precedence: parentheses beat everything; unary ! beats arithmetic; comparisons and logicals come last. When unsure, add parentheses.
Bitwise operators & | ^ ~ and shifts << >> >>> exist for low-level work — useful in performance-sensitive code and flags.
Ternary operator: condition ? ifTrue : ifFalse — a compact if/else expression that returns a value.
commonMistakes: Using = instead of == in comparisons — this is the classic bug; Java actually forbids it in most cases.
Forgetting integer division truncates: 7 / 2 == 3.
Expecting 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 to be true — it is false because of binary floating point.
Misusing i++ in expressions where ++i is intended, or vice versa.

title: Strings
analogy: A String is like a printed poster: once printed, you cannot edit a single letter — any 'change' produces a brand new poster. If you need to write on a whiteboard over and over, that's StringBuilder.
content: Strings are immutable: every method like toUpperCase(), trim(), or replace() returns a NEW String and leaves the original untouched.
String literals are interned: equal literals share the same object in the string pool, so == can be true for literals — but never rely on it for content comparison.
Use equals() (or equalsIgnoreCase()) for content comparison. == compares references.
Common methods: length(), charAt(i), substring(a,b), indexOf(x), contains(x), startsWith(x), endsWith(x), replace(a,b), split(regex), join(delimiter, parts).
String concatenation with + creates a new String each time — in loops this is O(n²). Use StringBuilder.append() for efficient building.
String.format() (and printf) let you build formatted output with %s, %d, %.2f placeholders.
Text blocks (Java 15+) with triple quotes """ preserve multi-line formatting for SQL, HTML, and long messages.
String transformations like strip(), repeat(n), and formatted() (Java 15+) add convenience for everyday work.
Parsing: Integer.parseInt(), Double.parseDouble(), Long.parseLong() convert text to numbers — they throw NumberFormatException on bad input.
commonMistakes: Comparing strings with == — always use equals().
Building strings in loops with + — use StringBuilder.
Assuming substring end index is inclusive — it is exclusive.
Calling split(".") and getting an empty array — . is a regex wildcard; use split("\\.").

title: If, Else, and Switch
analogy: Control flow is a train track with switches: an if/else switch sends the train down one branch; a switch statement is a junction box with many labeled tracks, each routing the train to exactly one destination.
content: if (condition) { ... } else if (...) { ... } else { ... } routes execution by boolean conditions.
Conditions must evaluate to boolean — unlike C, you cannot use a number as a condition.
Switch expressions (Java 14+) are the modern replacement for long if/else chains: switch (value) { case 1 -> ...; default -> ...; }
Traditional switch statements with case labels require break or they fall through to the next case.
Switch works with int, char, String, enums, and var types; case values must be compile-time constants.
The ternary operator ? : is an expression (returns a value), while if/else is a statement.
Nested conditionals are allowed but deep nesting hurts readability — extract methods or use early returns.
Guard clauses: check invalid inputs first and return early, so the happy path stays flat and readable.
Pattern matching for switch (Java 21 preview/stable in 21+): case String s when s.length() > 5 -> ... lets you match on type and bind variables.
commonMistakes: Writing if (x = 5) — assignment instead of comparison; it won't compile in Java, but if (x == 5) with single = is an eternal classic.
Forgetting break in traditional switch, causing fall-through.
Using == with floating point values that are computed, e.g. if (sum == 0.3).
Checking if (string.isEmpty()) vs (string == "") — use the method.

title: Loops
analogy: A loop is like a treadmill: the for loop is a treadmill with a preset timer and speed (init, condition, step), the while loop runs until you press the stop button, and the for-each is a conveyor belt where each item passes you exactly once.
content: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) — classic counting loop with initialization, condition, and update.
while (condition) { ... } — checks before each iteration; may run zero times.
do { ... } while (condition) — always runs at least once, then checks.
for-each (enhanced for): for (Type item : collection) — safe, readable iteration without index handling.
break exits the loop immediately; continue skips to the next iteration. Labeled break/continue (outer:) can exit nested loops.
Nested loops multiply complexity: watch for O(n²) patterns and off-by-one errors.
Common patterns: accumulating sums, finding min/max, counting matches, generating sequences (Fibonacci), and grid traversal.
Infinite loops happen when the condition never becomes false — usually a bug; while(true) is intentional only with an internal break.
Prefer for-each or streams for collections; use index-based for when you need the index or mutate positions.
commonMistakes: Off-by-one errors: using i <= length instead of i < length when indexing arrays.
Forgetting to update the loop variable in while loops — infinite loop.
Modifying a collection while iterating with for-each — throws ConcurrentModificationException.
Using i < array.length where length changes inside the loop body.

title: Arrays and Methods
analogy: An array is a row of lockers with numbers: locker 0, locker 1, locker 2... Each locker holds exactly one item of the same type, and you open it by its number. Methods are like vending-machine buttons: you press one, feed it inputs, and a defined behavior happens.
content: Arrays are fixed-size sequences: int[] numbers = new int[5]; or int[] nums = {10, 20, 30};
Indexing starts at 0; the last valid index is length - 1. Accessing outside throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
Default values: numeric arrays initialize to 0, boolean to false, char to '\u0000', reference types to null.
Multi-dimensional arrays are arrays of arrays: int[][] grid = new int[3][4];
Arrays are objects: array.length (no parentheses!) gives the size.
Arrays.toString() and Arrays.deepToString() produce readable output; Arrays.equals() and Arrays.compare() compare contents.
java.util.Arrays offers sort(), binarySearch(), fill(), copyOf(), and stream() for processing.
Methods: visibility (public/private/protected), static vs instance, return type, parameters — and the call stack where each call is a frame.
Method overloading: same name, different parameter lists. The compiler picks the most specific match.
Passing arrays to methods passes the reference — mutations inside the method are visible outside.
commonMistakes: Using array.length() instead of array.length — length is a field, not a method.
Off-by-one in loops: i <= arr.length causes an exception on the last iteration.
Assuming arrays from methods are copies — they are references; clone() or Arrays.copyOf() for real copies.
Using == to compare array contents — it compares references; use Arrays.equals().

title: Classes and Objects
analogy: A class is the blueprint for a car: it defines fields (engine size, color), methods (drive, brake), and the constructor is the factory that stamps out individual cars. Each car (object) has its own state, but they all follow the same blueprint.
content: A class defines fields (state) and methods (behavior). Objects are runtime instances created with new.
Encapsulation: keep fields private, expose controlled access through methods (getters/setters). This protects invariants.
The constructor initializes new objects; if you define no constructor, Java provides a no-arg one. A constructor is called exactly once per object.
this refers to the current object, resolving ambiguity between parameters and fields.
static members belong to the class, not instances: static int count and static void reset() are shared across all objects.
Fields have default values (0, false, null); local variables must be initialized explicitly.
Object identity vs equality: == checks identity (same reference), equals() compares logical value — override equals() and hashCode() together.
toString() gives a readable representation; the default is ClassName@hash — override it for meaningful logs.
Getters/setters can validate: setBalance(double amount) can reject negatives, protecting object invariants.
The 'new' keyword allocates memory on the heap; the garbage collector reclaims objects no longer referenced.
commonMistakes: Making fields public — breaks encapsulation and makes invariant protection impossible.
Naming the constructor with a different case than the class — it becomes a method, not a constructor.
Overriding equals() but not hashCode(), breaking HashMap behavior.
Using == on objects when you mean equals().

title: Inheritance and Polymorphism
analogy: Inheritance is like a restaurant's menu: the base class (a 'Dish') defines shared rules (has a name, a price). A subclass ('Pizza') adds its own toppings (fields and methods) and can override how it's described. The waiter (polymorphism) treats every dish the same way — plate it and serve it.
content: extends creates a subclass that inherits fields and methods from a superclass: class Car extends Vehicle.
The subclass adds or refines behavior; super.method() calls the parent implementation.
Constructor chaining: every constructor calls a superclass constructor — implicitly super() or explicitly super(args).
Method overriding: same signature, @Override annotation, and the most specific implementation runs (dynamic dispatch).
Overloading is compile-time (same name, different params); overriding is runtime (same signature).
Polymorphism: a reference of a parent type can hold any subclass — List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(); enables swapping implementations.
The 'is-a' rule: subclass is-a superclass. Composition ('has-a') is often better than inheritance for reuse.
final classes cannot be extended; final methods cannot be overridden.
Casting down: ((Car) vehicle).openTrunk() — check with instanceof first to avoid ClassCastException.
All classes ultimately inherit from Object, which provides toString(), equals(), hashCode(), getClass(), and clone().
Protected access: subclass code can access protected members of its superclass, private members cannot be inherited.
commonMistakes: Using inheritance for 'has-a' relationships (a Car HAS-A Engine, but Car extends Engine is wrong).
Forgetting to call super(args) when the superclass has no no-arg constructor.
Overriding without @Override — silent bugs when signatures drift.
Casting without instanceof and crashing with ClassCastException.

title: Interfaces and Abstract Classes
tagline: Design contracts, not just inheritance trees
analogy: An interface is a job posting: it says what you must do (methods to implement) but not how. An abstract class is a half-finished template: some parts are already built (concrete methods, fields), and you must fill in the blanks (abstract methods).
content: An interface is a contract: classes that implement it must provide all abstract methods. interface PaymentMethod { void pay(double amount); }
Since Java 8, interfaces can have default methods (implemented behavior with a default keyword) and static methods.
Interface fields are implicitly public static final — they are constants.
A class implements multiple interfaces, giving you a form of multiple inheritance of type.
An abstract class is declared with abstract and may contain concrete methods, fields, and constructors; abstract methods have no body and must be overridden.
Choose an interface when you define a capability/contract; choose an abstract class when you share state or partial implementation.
Functional interfaces have exactly one abstract method (Runnable, Comparator, Predicate) and can be used as lambdas.
Interfaces can extend other interfaces, building hierarchies: interface List<T> extends Collection<T>.
Sealed interfaces (Java 17+) restrict which classes may implement them, enabling exhaustive switch.
Default methods let you evolve an API without breaking implementers — e.g. List.sort() added in Java 8.
commonMistakes: Using an abstract class where an interface suffices, locking implementers into one parent.
Forgetting that interface constants are public static final and cannot be instance fields.
Implementing multiple interfaces with conflicting default methods and not overriding the conflict.
Declaring 'private' methods in interfaces before Java 9.

title: Polymorphism in Depth
analogy: Polymorphism is a universal remote: it says 'press Play', and each device (TV, projector, speaker) does its own thing. The remote (the interface) never changes; the devices behind it do.
content: Dynamic dispatch: at runtime, the JVM looks at the actual object type, not the reference type, to choose which method runs.
Virtual method tables (v-tables) are how the JVM implements this efficiently — each class carries a table of method pointers.
Upcasting (widening the type) is always safe: Dog d = ...; Animal a = d; works automatically.
Downcasting requires an explicit cast and an instanceof check: if (animal instanceof Dog dog) dog.fetch(); — pattern matching makes this elegant.
Interface polymorphism lets you swap implementations: PaymentMethod p = choosePayment(); — the calling code never changes.
Method resolution order: the most specific override wins; overloading is resolved at compile time by parameter types.
Covariant return types: an override may return a more specific type than the parent.
Polymorphism enables the Open/Closed principle: add new behavior by adding new classes, not by editing existing ones.
Pattern matching for instanceof (Java 16+) removes the cast boilerplate and scope variables cleanly.
Records, sealed hierarchies, and pattern matching together give Java algebraic-data-type style exhaustive switching.
commonMistakes: Casting blindly without instanceof and getting ClassCastException at runtime.
Expecting overloaded methods to dispatch dynamically — they do not; only overridden methods do.
Breaking the Liskov Substitution Principle: a subclass that throws where the parent doesn't breaks callers.
Designing huge inheritance trees when composition or interfaces would be simpler.

title: The Collections Framework
tagline: The Swiss Army knife of data storage
analogy: Imagine a toolbox with different drawers: a shelf where you slide tools in one by one (List), a labeled box where you grab tools by name (Map), and a bag that rejects duplicates (Set). Same toolbox, different drawers — each one optimized for a different job. The Collections Framework is that toolbox.
content: The Collections Framework is a set of interfaces and classes in java.util that handle groups of objects. The three root interfaces are List (ordered, allows duplicates), Set (no duplicates), and Map (key-value pairs).
List implementations: ArrayList (fast random access, backed by an array, O(1) get) and LinkedList (fast insert/remove at ends, O(n) get). For 95% of code, ArrayList wins.
Set implementations: HashSet (O(1) average, no order guaranteed), LinkedHashSet (keeps insertion order), TreeSet (sorted, O(log n) with Comparable).
Map implementations: HashMap (O(1) average lookup), LinkedHashMap (insertion order), TreeMap (sorted keys). Maps store key-value pairs; keys must be unique.

Iterate with an enhanced for loop, an iterator, or forEach(lambda). Never remove elements from a collection while for-looping — that throws ConcurrentModificationException; use iterator.remove() or removeIf().
Objects going into HashSet or as HashMap keys MUST implement equals() and hashCode() consistently, or lookups silently fail.
Collections utility class: sort, reverse, shuffle, max/min, unmodifiableList, binarySearch. It's a one-stop shop for common operations.
Autoboxing: int becomes Integer automatically, so collections of primitives work. Watch for nulls in boxed collections — unboxing a null throws NullPointerException.
Choose by operation: many lookups by key → HashMap; many lookups by index → ArrayList; unique sorted values → TreeSet; FIFO queue → ArrayDeque.
Prefer the interface type (List<String> list = new ArrayList<>()) so you can swap implementations without breaking code.
commonMistakes: Forgetting equals()/hashCode() on objects used in HashSet/HashMap — duplicates appear or lookups fail.
Modifying a collection while iterating with for-each: throws ConcurrentModificationException. Use removeIf or iterator.remove().
Using LinkedList everywhere because of its name — ArrayList is faster for most use cases.
Putting a mutable object into a HashSet and then mutating it — the bucket hash changes and the set becomes corrupt.
Forgetting that maps return null for missing keys — always check containsKey or use getOrDefault.

title: Generics: Type-Safe Containers
tagline: Let the compiler catch type bugs for you
analogy: Before generics, a collection was like a warehouse with no labels: you could drop a piano into the box marked 'screws' and only find out at the loading dock. Generics are the labels — the warehouse manager (compiler) now checks every item before it goes in.
content: Generics let you write classes and methods that work with any type while keeping type safety: List<String> can only hold Strings, enforced at compile time.
Type parameters are declared with angle brackets: class Box<T> or method <T> T pick(List<T> items). T is a placeholder replaced by the actual type when used.
The diamond operator lets you write List<String> list = new ArrayList<>() — Java infers the type from the left side.
Generic methods: <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(List<T> list) declares the type on the method, useful for utility methods and static helpers.
Bounded type parameters restrict what T can be: <T extends Number> accepts Integer, Double, etc., and you can call Number methods on T.
Wildcards handle unknown types: ? extends T (producer — you can only read) and ? super T (consumer — you can only write). Remember PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.
Type erasure: generics exist only at compile time. At runtime, List<String> and List<Integer> are both just List. This is why you cannot do new T() or check instanceof T.
Raw types (List without <>) compile with warnings and can cause ClassCastException at runtime — always use parameterized types.
Generics prevent entire classes of bugs: the compiler catches wrong-type insertions instead of crashing at runtime.
Arrays and generics don't mix well: new T[] is illegal because arrays know their component type at runtime but erasure erases T.
commonMistakes: Using raw types like List list = new ArrayList() — you lose all compile-time safety.
Trying to instantiate T with new T() or create new T[] — illegal due to erasure; pass a factory or Class<T> instead.
Confusing ? extends and ? super: extends is for reading (producers), super for writing (consumers).
Declaring <T extends Number> then assigning a String — the compiler rightly rejects it.
Overcomplicating signatures with wildcards where a plain T or concrete type would do — start simple.

title: Sets and Maps
analogy: A Set is a bouncer's list: everyone enters once, no repeat guests. A Map is a coat-check desk: hand over a token (key), get your coat (value) back instantly. Both rely on one superpower: knowing exactly which drawer to check — hashing.
content: A Set is a collection with no duplicates; adding an element that equals an existing one simply does nothing.
HashSet is backed by a hash table: each object's hashCode() decides its bucket, giving O(1) average add/contains/remove — but no guaranteed order.
The hashCode contract: if a.equals(b), then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(). Violating it breaks HashSet/HashMap lookups silently.
LinkedHashSet keeps insertion order with a doubly-linked list overlay — same O(1) performance, deterministic iteration.
TreeSet stores elements sorted (via natural Comparable order or a Comparator), giving O(log n) ops and range views like subSet(from, to).
A Map stores key-value pairs. HashMap gives O(1) average get/put; keys must override equals/hashCode.
Modern HashMap idioms: putIfAbsent, getOrDefault, computeIfAbsent (lazy value construction), merge (combine values).
TreeMap sorts by key, enabling firstKey/lastKey/floorKey/ceilingKey and range views — great for 'nearest match' problems.
Neither HashMap nor HashSet is thread-safe: concurrent modifications need ConcurrentHashMap or explicit synchronization.
Use EnumMap/EnumSet for enum keys/values — they are tiny arrays under the hood and absurdly fast.
commonMistakes: Using a mutable object (e.g., ArrayList) as a HashMap key, then mutating it — the entry becomes unfindable.
Forgetting equals()/hashCode() consistency on custom key classes.
Expecting HashSet to preserve insertion order — use LinkedHashSet if you need it.
Assuming HashMap iteration order — it is hash order, effectively random-looking.
Modifying a Set while iterating it — use iterator.remove() or removeIf.

title: Sorting: Comparable and Comparator
tagline: Two ways to teach Java your own order
analogy: Comparable is a person's 'natural order' — like alphabetical by last name in a phone book. Comparator is a custom sorting preference — today you want to sort by age, tomorrow by height. One is baked into the thing, the other is a plug-in rule you bring.
content: Comparable<T> gives a class one natural sort order by implementing int compareTo(T other) — used by Collections.sort, TreeSet, TreeMap, and Arrays.sort.
compareTo contract: return negative if this < other, zero if equal, positive if this > other. It must be transitive and consistent with equals().
Consistency with equals matters for Sets/Maps: if a.compareTo(b)==0 but !a.equals(b), TreeSet will still treat them as duplicates.
Comparator<T> is a separate strategy object letting you sort by any rule without touching the class — great for third-party or final classes.
Build comparators fluently: Comparator.comparing(Person::age).thenComparing(Person::name).reversed().
Handle nulls with nullsFirst()/nullsLast(), and avoid subtraction tricks (a-b) — integer overflow can silently corrupt the sort; use Integer.compare(a, b).
Sort lists with list.sort(comparator), sort arrays with Arrays.sort(arr, comparator), and streams with .sorted(comparator).
Records can implement Comparable for natural ordering: record Person(String name) implements Comparable<Person> with name-based compareTo.
Chained comparisons are the go-to for 'primary then secondary' rules (score desc, then name asc).
Comparator.comparingInt / comparingDouble avoid boxing overhead for primitives.
commonMistakes: Returning a - b in compareTo — overflows for large values; use Integer.compare(a, b).
Only implementing equals() but not Comparable, then wondering why TreeSet treats distinct objects as equal.
Forgetting .reversed() applies to the whole chain — call it on the base comparator before thenComparing.
Mutating a TreeSet element's sort key after insertion — the tree becomes inconsistent.
Using == instead of compareTo==0 to check ordering equality.

title: Enums: Fixed Sets of Constants
tagline: A type-safe switch for fixed options
analogy: An enum is like a light switch plate with a fixed set of positions: ON, OFF, DIMMED. You cannot invent a fourth position at runtime — the hardware simply doesn't have it. Strings can be misspelled and sneak past; an enum can't.
content: An enum declares a fixed, closed set of named constants: enum Day { MONDAY, TUESDAY, ... }. The compiler guarantees no other values exist.
Enums beat String/int constants: switch statements must handle every case (exhaustive), typos fail at compile time, and values are self-documenting.
Enum constants are singletons: Day.MONDAY is the only MONDAY that will ever exist, so == works reliably for comparison.
Each enum is a class: you can add fields, constructors, and methods. Constructor runs once per constant: enum Planet { EARTH(1.0), MARS(0.38); final double gravity; }

Built-in methods: values() returns all constants in declaration order, valueOf(name) resolves by exact name (throws IllegalArgumentException if unknown), ordinal() returns the declaration index (avoid relying on it).
Enums work great in switch statements, including the arrow syntax: case MONDAY, FRIDAY -> System.out.println("Work");
EnumMap and EnumSet are ultra-fast collections specialized for enum keys/values — use them instead of HashMap for enums.
Enums can implement interfaces, letting different constants behave differently — a neat polymorphic pattern.
Since Java 17 enums can be sealed-like: they are implicitly final and cannot be extended.
Use enums for status codes, roles, card suits, directions, config options — anything with a known finite set.
commonMistakes: Using String constants like "ACTIVE" / "active" — one typo silently breaks logic; enums make typos compile errors.
Calling valueOf with the wrong case or a nonexistent name — throws IllegalArgumentException. Handle or catch it.
Depending on ordinal() for persistence — reordering constants changes ordinals; store an explicit id field instead.
Adding methods that mutate fields — enum constants should stay effectively immutable.
Forgetting trailing semicolon when an enum has fields/methods after the constant list.

title: Records: Data Carriers
analogy: A record is like a photo of an object: capture it once, and it never changes. Before records, writing a simple data holder meant hand-typing fields, getters, equals, hashCode, and toString — 60 lines of boilerplate. Now it's one line, and it's a promise of immutability.
content: A record is a transparent, immutable carrier for data: record Point(int x, int y) gives you fields, accessors x() and y(), equals, hashCode, and toString for free.
Records are final classes — they cannot be extended, and their fields are private final. The only public constructor is the canonical one.
Accessors have no 'get' prefix: point.x(), not point.getX(). A common gotcha for developers from older Java styles.
You can add a compact constructor to validate: record Age(int years) { Age { if (years < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); } } — parameters are auto-assigned after the body.
You can add extra methods and static factories, but you cannot add extra instance fields.
Two records are equal if they are the same type and all components are equal — equals/hashCode are derived from components.
Records combine beautifully with patterns: if (obj instanceof Point p) — pattern matching gives you the components without casting.
Use records for DTOs, API responses, method return pairs, map keys — anywhere you need immutable grouped data.
Records work with generics and can implement interfaces: record Pair<A, B>(A a, B b) implements Comparable<Pair<A, B>>.
A local record declared inside a method is a handy way to bundle intermediate results without polluting the codebase.
commonMistakes: Looking for getX() methods — records use accessors named after components (x()).
Trying to extend a record or add instance fields — both are illegal by design.
Forgetting records are immutable: there are no setters. Build a new record to change data.
Using records for mutable state carriers — they are for data, not behavior.
Validation with non-compact constructors re-declaring every parameter — the compact constructor is the cleaner idiom.

title: Optional: Taming null
analogy: A null is a doctor leaving the room without saying anything. Optional is a labelled envelope: either it contains a result, or it's empty — but you always know which. The type system itself reminds you to check before opening.
content: Optional<T> is a wrapper that is either present or empty — the type signature says 'this value may not exist', making null handling explicit instead of accidental.
Create with Optional.of(value) (throws NPE on null), Optional.ofNullable(value) (empty for null), or Optional.empty().
Read safely: ifPresent(v -> ...), orElse(default), orElseGet(() -> expensive()) — orElseGet evaluates lazily, so use it when the default is costly to build.
Transform with map and filter: opt.map(String::toUpperCase).filter(s -> s.length() > 3) chains without null checks.
flatMap flattens nested Optionals: findUser(id).flatMap(User::getEmail) keeps one level of Optional instead of Optional<Optional<...>>.
Throw on empty with orElseThrow() (NoSuchElementException) or orElseThrow(() -> new CustomException()).
Do NOT use Optional for fields, method parameters, or collection elements — it is designed for return types only, and serializing it is a pain.
Prefer returning Optional over returning null from your own lookup methods — callers can then handle emptiness with the fluent API.
Beware of orElse with side effects — the default is evaluated eagerly even when the value is present.
Optional works with streams: stream.filter(Optional::isPresent).map(Optional::get), or even better, flatMap(Optional::stream) in newer Java.
commonMistakes: Using Optional.of(value) with a possibly-null value — it throws. ofNullable is the safe choice.
Calling .get() without checking isPresent() — that reintroduces the null-style crash with worse errors.
Using orElse(costlyDefault()) — the default is built eagerly; use orElseGet for lazy defaults.
Storing Optionals in fields/collections — it bloats memory and complicates code; use Optional only for returns.
Returning null from methods whose callers expect Optional — always return Optional.empty() instead.

title: Lambdas and Functional Interfaces
analogy: Before lambdas, passing behavior meant wrapping it in a verbose anonymous class — like mailing a whole envelope when you only needed to write one sentence inside. A lambda is that sentence: you pass the behavior itself, directly.
content: A lambda is a compact anonymous function: (a, b) -> a + b. It implements a functional interface — an interface with exactly one abstract method.
Functional interfaces are marked @FunctionalInterface (optional but self-documenting); Runnable, Comparator, Callable are the classic JDK ones.
The core java.util.function interfaces: Predicate<T> (T -> boolean), Function<T, R> (T -> R), Consumer<T> (T -> void), Supplier<T> (() -> T), BiFunction, UnaryOperator.
Syntax: parameter types are optional when inferable, parentheses optional for single params: s -> s.length() works.
A lambda captures effectively-final local variables — variables it uses must never be reassigned after initialization (or after the lambda).
Lambdas beat anonymous classes in readability and performance (invokedynamic, no extra class file per usage).
Under the hood a lambda compiles to a hidden method invoked via invokedynamic — still just a functional interface at the type level.
You can chain the core interfaces: Function.compose/andThen, Predicate.and/or/negate, Consumer.andThen.
Lambdas enable the strategy pattern elegantly: pass different sorting rules, predicates, or error handlers to the same method.
Know the runtime cost is ~zero for creation; use lambdas freely wherever a functional interface is expected.
commonMistakes: Reassigning a variable captured by a lambda — compile error 'variable used in lambda should be effectively final'. Copy it to a new local if you must.
Forgetting that a lambda with multiple statements needs braces and explicit return: (a, b) -> { int c = a + b; return c; }.
Using a lambda where no functional interface is expected — it won't compile; the target type must be an interface with one abstract method.
Side effects inside lambdas (mutating captured objects) — legal but makes code unpredictable and hard to debug.
Ambiguous lambda types when overloaded methods could match two different functional interfaces — add explicit casts or assign to a typed variable.

title: Streams: Declarative Data Processing
analogy: A stream is like an assembly line at a factory: items come in one end, pass through stations (filter removes bad parts, map changes each part, sort arranges them), and a terminal station collects the output. Each item travels the line once, in order, and no station starts work until the output is actually requested.
content: A stream is a pipeline of operations over a sequence of elements — it is NOT a data structure; it never stores data.
Structure: source (list.stream()), zero or more intermediate ops (map, filter, sorted, distinct, limit), then exactly one terminal op (toList, count, reduce, forEach).
Intermediate operations are lazy — nothing runs until a terminal operation is invoked. This enables short-circuiting like limit(3) and anyMatch.
map transforms each element (String -> length), filter keeps matches, sorted orders, distinct removes duplicates, limit/skip cap the pipeline.
Terminal ops: toList(), count(), reduce(identity, accumulator), min/max, anyMatch/allMatch/noneMatch, forEach, findFirst.
Streams never mutate the source collection — they produce new results, which makes pipelines safe and side-effect-free (when done right).
IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream avoid boxing: IntStream.range(1, 5), .sum(), .average(), .summaryStatistics().
Prefer streams for readable transformation chains; prefer loops when you need early exit with complex state or lots of side effects.
Strings of a file can be streamed (Files.lines) to process large files lazily without loading them into memory.
Collect into mutable containers with .collect(Collectors.toList()) or the newer .toList() (immutable, Java 16+).
commonMistakes: Forgetting a terminal operation — without one, the pipeline never executes and nothing happens.
Reusing a stream after a terminal operation — IllegalStateException 'stream has already been operated upon'. Create a new stream each time.
Mutating the source collection inside a stream (e.g., list.removeIf inside forEach) — causes concurrent modification failures.
Using parallel() carelessly — ordering guarantees vanish and shared state becomes a race.
Reaching for streams when a simple loop with early break is clearer — streams are elegant, not mandatory.

title: Advanced Streams: Collectors
analogy: If basic streams are an assembly line, collectors are the sorting bins at the end of the line. One bin organizes items into labeled groups (groupingBy), another splits them into two piles (partitioningBy), another joins all the labels into a single banner (joining).
content: Collectors are terminal operations that gather stream elements into rich results: lists, sets, maps, strings, and summarized statistics.
Collectors.groupingBy(classifier) returns Map<K, List<V>>: group words by first letter, orders by key (preserves encounter order for the lists).
groupingBy with a downstream collector refines the groups: groupingBy(word::length, counting()) gives Map<Integer, Long> of length -> count.
partitioningBy(predicate) is groupingBy with exactly two buckets: true and false — perfect for pass/fail splits.
joining() concatenates strings (optionally with delimiter/prefix/suffix): Collectors.joining(", ") turns a list into "a, b, c".
summarizingInt / summarizingDouble produce count, sum, min, average, max in one pass — great for dashboards.
toMap(keyMapper, valueMapper) has a killer overload with a merge function to resolve duplicate keys: toMap(word, String::length, Math::max).
flatMap flattens nested structures: List<List<Integer>> becomes one stream of Integer; also List<Optional<T>>.flatMap(Optional::stream).
Streams can run in parallel: list.parallelStream() — but only when the pipeline is stateless, order-insensitive, and the data set is large enough to matter.
peek() is a debug-only op for observing elements as they flow through — never rely on it for side effects in production logic.
teeing() (Java 12+) sends elements to two collectors and combines their results — a mini fork-join for streams.
takeWhile/dropWhile (Java 9+) cut the pipeline once a condition flips — like limit but predicate-driven.
commonMistakes: groupingBy producing unordered groups when you need sorted keys — chain .collect(...) then sort, or collect into a TreeMap via groupingBy(key, TreeMap::new, downstream).
toMap with duplicate keys throwing IllegalStateException — always provide a merge function when keys can repeat.
Calling parallel() on small or ordered pipelines — overhead exceeds gains and order becomes unspecified.
Using peek for production side effects — it is a debugging tool; use map or forEach instead.
Collecting a parallel stream into a mutable shared container with forEach — race conditions; use collect() which is thread-safe.

title: Method References and Composition
analogy: A method reference is shorthand: instead of writing a full recipe each time (s -> s.toUpperCase()), you point to the cookbook page (String::toUpperCase). Same dish, less handwriting. Composition chains mini-recipes into one grand recipe.
content: A method reference is a compact lambda: Class::staticMethod, object::instanceMethod, Class::instanceMethod, or Class::new.
The four kinds: String::valueOf (static), list::add (instance on an existing object), String::toUpperCase (instance on any argument — 'unbound'), ArrayList::new (constructor).
Method references work wherever a lambda is expected, provided signatures match — the compiler checks the target functional interface.
Instance-on-arbitrary-type references (Class::instanceMethod) turn 'the argument becomes the receiver': names.stream().map(String::toUpperCase).
Constructor references (Type::new) are great factories: List<Person> = names.stream().map(Person::new).toList().
Function composition: f.andThen(g) runs f then g; f.compose(g) runs g then f — 'compose' reads right-to-left, so say it aloud before using it.
Predicate composition: p.and(q), p.or(r), p.negate() build complex conditions without a single if statement.
Composed chains stay lazy and read like a sentence: filter(s -> !s.isEmpty()).map(String::trim).map(String::toLowerCase).
Reference a method on an effectively-final captured object: printer::print — handy for logging and callbacks.
Use method references when they read naturally; keep lambdas when logic needs local variables or multiple statements.
commonMistakes: Using instance-method references where the object varies — String::toUpperCase means 'call on each argument', not 'call on one fixed string'.
Confusing compose order: f.compose(g) applies g first. When in doubt, chain with andThen and read left to right.
Writing Person::new for a record/class whose constructor signature doesn't match the functional interface — mismatch is a compile error.
Reference to a mutable captured object — the reference holds whatever the object currently is; fine for final, confusing otherwise.
Overusing references until code becomes cryptic — a short lambda often reads better than a hyper-short reference.

title: Exceptions: Handling the Unexpected
analogy: An exception is a smoke detector: when something goes wrong, it doesn't burn the whole house down silently — it sounds the alarm (throws), and you either deal with the fire (catch) or let the fire department (the caller) handle it. Java forces you to acknowledge the alarm.
content: An exception is an event that disrupts normal program flow, represented by an object of a subclass of Throwable. Three families: Error (JVM problems, don't catch), Exception (recoverable), RuntimeException (a.k.a. unchecked).

Checked exceptions (IOException, SQLException) must be declared with throws or handled with try/catch — the compiler enforces this. Unchecked exceptions (NullPointerException, ArithmeticException) are programming bugs, not required to be handled.
try/catch/finally: try runs risky code, catch handles specific exception types, finally always runs (even on return or exception) — ideal for cleanup like closing resources.
Catch order matters: more specific exception types must come first (e.g., FileNotFoundException before IOException), or the compiler refuses to compile.
A single catch can handle multiple types with the multi-catch pipe: catch (IOException | NumberFormatException e).
Throw your own with throw new IllegalArgumentException("...") and declare checked ones with throws on the method signature.
The stack trace (read bottom-up for the root cause... actually read top-down for the failure point, then find the first frame in YOUR code) is your best debugging map.
Never swallow exceptions with empty catch blocks — at minimum log or rethrow; silent failures are the worst bugs.
catch (Exception e) is a code smell — catch the specific exception you can actually handle.

Common unchecked exceptions: NullPointerException (call on null), ArithmeticException (divide by zero), IndexOutOfBoundsException (bad array index), IllegalArgumentException (bad argument), NumberFormatException (bad parse).
commonMistakes: Empty catch blocks that swallow errors — the program 'works' until the silent bug bites in production.
Catching Exception or Throwable broadly — you hide bugs and can't tell what actually failed.
Ordering catch blocks wrong: catch (IOException e) before catch (FileNotFoundException e) won't compile.
Forgetting that finally runs even when return executes before it — cleanup placed after the try is skipped on exceptions.
Declaring throws on main() for everything — handled exceptions give users a graceful message instead of a crash.

title: Advanced Exception Handling
analogy: A good restaurant doesn't just cook food — it cleans up the table no matter what happens (try-with-resources does the cleaning automatically). And when a kitchen problem is unusual, the chef writes their own special menu item: a custom exception, so waiters (callers) know exactly what went wrong.
content: try-with-resources auto-closes any resource implementing AutoCloseable, guaranteeing cleanup even on exceptions: try (BufferedReader r = Files.newBufferedReader(p)) { ... }.
Resources are closed in reverse order of declaration, and close() failures become suppressed exceptions — visible via getSuppressed().
Multi-catch lets you handle unrelated exceptions uniformly: catch (IOException | SQLException e) — no 'related by subclass' allowed in one clause.
Exception chaining preserves the original cause: catch (IOException e) { throw new StorageException("save failed", e); } — callers see getCause().
Write custom exceptions by extending Exception (checked) or RuntimeException (unchecked). Unchecked for programmer errors; checked for environmental failures you want callers forced to handle.
Custom exceptions should provide good constructors (message, cause) and a descriptive name: OrderNotFoundException beats Exception.
Rethrow idiom: catch and wrap when you cross abstraction layers (SQLException -> RepositoryException), so UI code doesn't leak persistence details.
Fail fast: validate arguments at the top of methods (Objects.requireNonNull, explicit checks) before touching state.
The 'picky' rule: only catch what you can meaningfully handle. Otherwise, let it propagate to the layer that can.
Assertions (assert) are for internal invariants in development, not user input validation — remove them from production paths.
commonMistakes: Writing a custom exception that extends Exception for programmer bugs — unchecked (RuntimeException) is usually right for those.
Losing the root cause: throwing new RuntimeException("failed") without chaining the original — always pass the cause.
Manual close() in finally when try-with-resources would do it — more code, more ways to fail.
Multi-catch clauses with related exception types — won't compile; catch the parent once instead.
Returning null on failure instead of throwing — pushes the failure to every caller to remember to check.

title: File I/O with NIO.2
tagline: Read and write files the modern way
analogy: Think of the filesystem as a huge library. NIO.2 is the librarian: Path is the call number, Files is the shelf you walk to. The old java.io API made you carry every book by hand; NIO.2 gives you a cart — one method reads a whole shelf.
content: NIO.2 (java.nio.file) is the modern I/O API. The two stars: Path (a file or directory location) and Files (static methods that operate on paths).
Create paths: Path.of("data", "notes.txt") or Paths.get(...). Paths are platform-independent — never hardcode separators like \\; use Path.of.
Read everything: Files.readAllLines(path) (List<String>), Files.readString(path), Files.writeString(path, text) — one-liners for small files.
Stream files for large data: try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(path)) — processes line by line without loading the whole file into memory.
File ops: Files.exists, Files.copy (with REPLACE_EXISTING), Files.move, Files.delete (throws if missing; deleteIfExists returns boolean), Files.createDirectories for nested dirs.
Wrap readers/writers for control: BufferedReader/Files.newBufferedReader for line-by-line reading, BufferedWriter for writing — always inside try-with-resources.
Directory listing: Files.list(dir) streams entries (remember to close it!), Files.walk(dir) descends recursively.
Check metadata: Files.size, Files.isDirectory, Files.getLastModifiedTime, Files.isRegularFile.
Charsets matter: Files.readString defaults to UTF-8; for other encodings pass StandardCharsets explicitly.
All these methods throw IOException (a checked exception) — handle it with try/catch or declare throws. That's the compiler forcing you to plan for failure.
commonMistakes: Building paths with string concatenation ("data/" + name) — breaks on Windows separators; use Path.of/Paths.get and resolve().
Forgetting Files.lines() and Files.list() return streams that must be closed — wrap them in try-with-resources.
Calling Files.delete on a missing file and crashing — use deleteIfExists or check first.
Using readAllLines on a 2 GB log file — memory blowup; stream it with Files.lines instead.
Ignoring IOException in a way that breaks the app — silent catches again; log or rethrow with context.

title: Dates and Times with java.time
analogy: Old java.util.Date was a Swiss watch with no face: it stored milliseconds since 1970 but confused dates, times, and timezones. java.time is three separate clocks on one wall: LocalDate (the calendar), LocalTime (the stopwatch), and Instant (the atomic-clock timestamp for machines).
content: java.time (Java 8+) replaced the confusing java.util.Date/Calendar. The core classes are immutable and thread-safe — methods return new instances.
LocalDate stores a date (year-month-day), LocalTime stores a time, LocalDateTime both. No timezone — for human calendars and schedules.
Instant is a timestamp on the UTC timeline — what machines and databases love. Convert with Instant.now() and Date/Instant bridges.
ZonedDateTime pairs a local date-time with a ZoneId (e.g., ZoneId.of("Europe/Paris")) — use it for actual global timestamps.
Construct via static factories: LocalDate.of(2024, 3, 14), .now(), .parse("2024-03-14"). No more new Date(2024, 3, 14) off-by-one madness.
Arithmetic returns new instances: date.plusDays(1), date.minusMonths(2), time.plusMinutes(30) — chainable and safe.
Compare with isBefore/isAfter/compareTo/equals — LocalDate.now().isBefore(deadline) reads like English.
Duration measures time (hours/minutes/seconds), Period measures calendar time (years/months/days). Difference: Duration.between(t1, t2).
Format and parse with DateTimeFormatter: LocalDate.parse("14/03/2024", DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd/MM/yyyy")). Formatters are thread-safe constants.
TemporalAdjusters offer calendar logic: .with(TemporalAdjusters.lastDayOfMonth()), firstDayOfNextMonth — no manual day math.
DayOfWeek, Month, Year are first-class enums: date.getDayOfWeek() gives DayOfWeek.MONDAY, testable with == or getValue().
commonMistakes: Using java.util.Date/Calendar — legacy, mutable, and confusing. Everything has a java.time equivalent.
Assuming LocalDate.now() has a timezone — it's the JVM default zone's date; use ZonedDateTime/Instant for global correctness.
Date arithmetic with plusDays off by one because of month boundaries — java.time handles it; trust it.
Parsing with the wrong pattern — DateTimeParseException; test your pattern before shipping.
Mixing Duration and Period: two hours vs two months aren't the same kind of thing.

title: Reflection and Annotations
tagline: Code that inspects and decorates code
analogy: Reflection is a mirror the program holds up to itself: it can read its own class names, methods, and fields at runtime. Annotations are sticky notes you place on code ("@Deprecated", "@Override") that tools and frameworks read to change behavior without touching the code itself.
content: Reflection (java.lang.reflect) lets a running program inspect its own classes: get names, fields, methods, constructors, and even invoke them at runtime.
Get a Class object three ways: Class.forName("com.example.Person"), Person.class, or obj.getClass(). All three are equal for the same class.
Inspect members: clazz.getDeclaredMethods(), getDeclaredFields(), getConstructors() return their Java-object representations with names and modifiers.
Invoke dynamically: method.setAccessible(true) then method.invoke(instance, args) — this is how frameworks call your methods without knowing them at compile time.
Reflection is powerful but slow and fragile: mistakes surface as runtime exceptions, not compile errors. Reserve it for frameworks and tooling.
Annotations are metadata: @Override (compiler check), @Deprecated (warnings), @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") — these three are built in.
Custom annotations: @interface Tag { String value(); } optionally annotated with @Retention and @Target to control when they exist and where they're legal.
@Retention(RUNTIME) makes an annotation visible to reflection; CLASS (default) is in bytecode but not readable at runtime; SOURCE disappears at compile.
Reading annotations with reflection: clazz.getAnnotation(Tag.class) or method.getAnnotations() — this is the engine behind JUnit, Spring, and ORMs.
Real-world pattern: frameworks scan classes for annotations, then use reflection to wire behavior — JUnit finds @Test methods, Jackson maps @JsonProperty fields.
commonMistakes: Using reflection for normal application code — compile-time types and method calls are faster, safer, and clearer.
Ignoring checked exceptions reflection throws (ClassNotFoundException, InvocationTargetException, IllegalAccessException).
Forgetting setAccessible(true) before invoking private members (fails on some JDK configurations).
Assuming class names from strings won't break — one typo in Class.forName becomes a runtime crash.
Creating custom annotations without @Retention(RUNTIME) then wondering why reflection can't see them.

title: Threads: Running Code in Parallel
tagline: Do many things at once — safely
analogy: A single thread is one chef in a kitchen: one dish at a time. Threads are a team of chefs: the team cooks faster, but if two chefs grab the same pan (shared variable) at once, the soup ends up in the salad. Coordination is the art.
content: A thread is the smallest unit of execution. The JVM starts with the main thread; you create more with new Thread(runnable) and start them with .start() — never call run() directly (that just runs it on the current thread).
The Runnable interface is the classic job description: run() holds the work. Lambdas make this one line: Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println("hi"));
Thread lifecycle states: NEW (created), RUNNABLE (running or ready), BLOCKED (waiting for a lock), WAITING, TIMED_WAITING (sleep/join), TERMINATED (done).
Order is nondeterministic: scheduling decides which thread runs when. Never assume 'first started = first finished'.
Join to wait: thread.join() blocks the caller until that thread finishes — the simplest way to collect results.
Thread.sleep(ms) pauses a thread (checked InterruptedException) — use it to simulate work or throttle, not to synchronize.
Interrupt is a polite request to stop: interrupt() sets a flag; cooperative code checks Thread.interrupted() or catches InterruptedException and cleans up.
The dreaded race condition: two threads reading/writing shared mutable state interleave — the classic counter++ is two instructions (read, write) and can lose increments.
For safety: minimize shared mutable state, use immutable data (records!), or synchronize access — more on that next lesson.
Daemon threads (t.setDaemon(true)) don't keep the JVM alive — background housekeeping dies when the main thread exits.
Prefer modern tools (Executors, CompletableFuture) over raw threads for real work — they manage pools and failure for you.
commonMistakes: Calling run() instead of start() — it runs on the caller's thread, no parallelism at all.
Starting the same thread twice — IllegalThreadStateException. Create a new Thread each time.
Expecting deterministic output order — scheduling is up to the OS; interleave is normal.
Forgetting to join() and watching the main thread finish before workers — results vanish.
Sharing mutable state without synchronization — the silent counter-losing-increments class of bugs.

exercises.title: Parallel countdown
exercises.prompt: Start three threads that each count down from 3 to 1, with names, and have main wait for all of them.

exercises.title: Race detector
exercises.prompt: Create 1,000 threads that each increment a shared int counter 1,000 times. Print the final value — it won't be 1,000,000. Why?

title: Synchronization and Locks
tagline: Make shared state safe to share
analogy: A bathroom with a lock: only one person inside at a time (synchronized). Everyone else queues outside (BLOCKED state). The lock is not a wall — it only works if everyone agrees to use it. And if two bathrooms lock each other's doors... that's a deadlock.
content: A race condition happens when read-modify-write sequences from multiple threads interleave. The fix: mutual exclusion — only one thread in the critical section at a time.
synchronized on a method locks the instance (this); synchronized on a static method locks the class; a synchronized(lock) block lets you lock any object.
Intrinsic locks are reentrant: a thread holding the lock can re-enter other synchronized methods on the same object — no self-deadlock.
volatile guarantees visibility: writes to a volatile field are immediately seen by other threads. It fixes staleness, NOT atomicity — counter++ still races with volatile alone.
Atomic classes (java.util.concurrent.atomic): AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicReference give lock-free atomic operations via CAS (compare-and-set).
Explicit locks: ReentrantLock with lock()/unlock() (finally-guarded!) supports tryLock(timeout) to avoid blocking forever, and fairness options.
Deadlock: threads hold locks and wait for each other's — classic example: thread A holds lock1 wants lock2, thread B holds lock2 wants lock1. Everyone hangs.
Deadlock avoidance: acquire locks in a consistent global order, use tryLock with timeouts, or minimize lock scope.
The happens-before guarantee: releasing a lock makes all previous writes visible to the next thread that acquires it.
Strategy ladder: prefer immutability (no locking!), then atomic classes, then synchronization; reach for Locks only when you need tryLock/timeouts.
commonMistakes: Relying on volatile for compound operations — it fixes visibility, not atomicity. Use atomics or synchronized.
Locking more than needed (whole method vs. minimal block) — throughput tanks; keep critical sections tiny.
Forgetting to unlock in finally with ReentrantLock — one exception and the lock is stuck forever.
Two locks acquired in inconsistent order — the classic deadlock recipe. Pick one global order.
Synchronizing on mutable objects or String literals — you may share locks you don't know you share.

exercises.title: Fix the race
exercises.prompt: Take the counter race from the last lesson and fix it with a synchronized block; verify the total is exactly 1,000,000.

exercises.title: Atomic stats
exercises.prompt: Use AtomicLong to compute a total across 10 threads each adding 1..1000, then print the result.

title: Executors and CompletableFuture
analogy: Creating a thread per task is like hiring a new employee per chore — expensive and chaotic. An ExecutorService is a fixed team of employees (a pool) that processes a queue of tasks. CompletableFuture is a project manager who chains tasks: 'when the report is ready, email it, then log it'.
content: ExecutorService decouples task submission from thread management: submit tasks, and a pool of threads (newFixedThreadPool(n), newCachedThreadPool(), newSingleThreadExecutor()) runs them.
submit() returns a Future<T>: a handle to the eventual result. future.get() blocks until it's ready (and rethrows the task's exception as ExecutionException).
Shut down properly: shutdown() (no new tasks, finish queued) vs shutdownNow() (interrupt in-flight). Leaked pools keep the JVM alive.
Callable<T> is Runnable that returns a value (and can throw) — submit Callable to get results, plain Runnable when you don't need them.
CompletableFuture brings async pipelines: supplyAsync(() -> compute()) then .thenApply(transform).thenAccept(consume) — no blocking in between.
Compose futures: thenCompose chains one future's result into a new async task (flatMap for futures); thenCombine merges two results (zip).
Handle failure: exceptionally(e -> fallbackValue) or handle((result, error) -> ...) — the async try/catch.
Fan out with allOf(f1, f2, f3) (wait for all) and anyOf (first success) — parallel branching made readable.
Concurrent collections: ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentLinkedQueue give safe shared structures without manual locking.
invokeAll(collection of Callables) runs them all and returns their futures — a clean parallel-for idiom.
Structured concurrency (Java 21) is the future: tasks inherit scope, are cancelled together; prefer it for new greenfield code.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to shutdown the pool — the JVM never exits; use try-with-resources style or shutdown in finally.
Calling .get() on a Future inside a UI/main thread without care — it blocks; that's fine in main, deadly in a web request thread.
Blocking .get() on a CompletableFuture you could have composed — pipelines should stay async.
Sharing mutable state across parallel tasks — use ConcurrentHashMap/atomics or make tasks independent.
Creating a new pool per task — pool creation is expensive; reuse pools (or the common pool).

exercises.title: Parallel array max
exercises.prompt: Split a large array into 4 parts, compute each part's max in parallel with a pool of 4, then combine results.

exercises.title: Async greeting
exercises.prompt: Use CompletableFuture to fetch a name asynchronously (simulate with sleep), then produce a greeting, all without blocking in main except the final get.

title: Inside the JVM
analogy: The JVM is a universal translator: your .java source is translated into a lingua franca (bytecode) that any machine speaking any dialect can read. Your app runs in a well-guarded embassy (the JVM) that manages its own water supply (heap) and hires cleaners (the garbage collector) who take out the trash automatically.
content: Compile once, run anywhere: javac compiles .java to .class bytecode; any JVM (Windows, Linux, Mac, phone) runs the same bytecode.
Inspect bytecode with the JDK's javap tool: javap -c MyClass shows the JVM instructions your source compiles into.
The JVM has separate memory areas: heap (objects, shared by all threads), method area (class definitions, static fields), per-thread stacks (method frames, locals), and program counters.
The heap is split into generations: young (Eden + survivor spaces — new objects) and old (long-lived objects). Most objects die young.
Garbage collection (GC) reclaims unreachable objects automatically: minor GCs clean the young gen, major/full GCs the old gen. The GC, not you, frees memory.
Common collectors: G1 (default since 9 — low pauses, region-based) and ZGC (ultra-low-pause, for huge heaps). You rarely configure them; the JVM picks sane defaults.
JVM flags: -Xmx2g (max heap), -Xms512m (initial heap), -verbose:gc (watch collections), -Xlog:gc (modern logging). Wrong heap size is a top production cause of OOM or wasted memory.
The string pool interns string literals: "duke" == "duke" is true because literals are shared; new String("duke") is a fresh object on the heap.
Class loading: the bootstrap (JDK core), platform, and application classloaders load classes on first use, delegation-first (parent loads before child).
Class initialization runs static blocks once, on first active use — that's why static state feels like a singleton.
OutOfMemoryError means the heap is full — usually a leak (unbounded static collections, listeners never removed), not 'too many objects' — learn to read -Xlog:gc and use a profiler.
commonMistakes: Thinking you must call System.gc() — it's a hint, often ignored; the JVM manages collection timing.
Comparing strings with == outside the literal-pool case — always equals() for content.
Assuming more heap (-Xmx) always helps — oversized heaps lengthen GC pauses; measure first.
Ignoring OutOfMemoryError as a JVM issue when it's usually an application leak.
Tuning GC flags from blog posts without profiling — the defaults are excellent for most apps.

exercises.title: Memory explorer
exercises.prompt: Print heap usage, create a big List, print usage again, then after clearing, note what changed. Also print max heap and CPU count.

exercises.title: String pool detective
exercises.prompt: Predict and verify which == comparisons are true (literals, concatenated literals, new String, intern()).

title: Build Tools: Maven and Gradle
analogy: Writing Java without a build tool is like running a restaurant with no supplier: you'd hand-pick every ingredient (library) yourself, store them in jars, and re-boil the same recipes each morning. Maven/Gradle are your automated suppliers and recipe manager: declare what you need, and they fetch, organize, and build it.
content: A build tool compiles, tests, packages, and resolves dependencies automatically — the foundation of every real Java project.
Maven's contract: a standard directory layout (src/main/java, src/main/resources, src/test/java) so every Maven project looks alike.
The pom.xml declares the project: groupId:artifactId:version (Maven coordinates), plus <dependencies> with the same coordinates and a scope (compile, test, provided).
Dependencies are downloaded from central repositories (Maven Central) — you never vendor jar files yourself anymore.
The Maven lifecycle: validate -> compile -> test -> package -> install. mvn test runs your tests; mvn package produces a jar/war.
Gradle does the same job with a Groovy/Kotlin DSL (build.gradle) and is faster (incremental builds, caching, daemon) — Android's build tool.

Dependency management handles transitive dependencies: your library's dependencies arrive automatically, and conflicts are resolved to a single version (nearest-wins in Maven; richer resolution in Gradle).
Version conflicts are the #1 build headache: exclusions, dependency management/dependencyConstraints, and lockfiles tame them.
What your IDE actually does when you press Run: it invokes the build tool under the hood — knowing the CLI makes you IDE-independent.
jar = Java ARchive: a zip of .class files plus a manifest. The 'fat jar' pattern bundles dependencies so java -jar app.jar just works.
commonMistakes: Hardcoding library versions in multiple places — use a properties block (<properties>) or BOM to define versions once.
Committing downloaded jars to the repo — the build tool fetches them; only the manifest (pom/build.gradle) should be versioned.
Ignoring dependency conflicts until runtime NoClassDefFoundError — inspect the dependency tree early (mvn dependency:tree).
Assuming mvn compile also runs tests — the lifecycle steps are sequential; run mvn test or mvn verify for the full pipeline.
Deleting build/ or target/ and panicking — they're regenerated artifacts, safe to delete.

exercises.title: Project layout planner
exercises.prompt: Print the standard Maven directory structure and, for each directory, state what belongs there.

exercises.title: Dependency checklist
exercises.prompt: Given a list of dependencies (name, version, scope), print only the compile-scope ones.

title: JDBC: Talking to Databases
analogy: JDBC is a telephone exchange between Java and databases: your code dials (DriverManager), gets a connection (Connection), and sends prepared letters (PreparedStatement) to a receptionist who answers with pages of results (ResultSet). The exchange works with any phone company (database) that speaks the same standard.
content: JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) is the standard API for database access. It works across vendors: the same code runs on H2, PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite — you only swap the driver dependency.
The cast: DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pass) hands you a Connection. The URL is vendor-specific, e.g. jdbc:postgresql://localhost/db or jdbc:h2:mem:test.
Statement vs PreparedStatement: always use PreparedStatement — it escapes values (blocks SQL injection) and caches execution plans for performance.
SQL injection is the classic bug: building SQL by string concatenation ("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='" + name + "'") lets a user's input rewrite your query. Parameters (?) fix it forever.
Querying: preparedStatement.executeQuery() returns a ResultSet; iterate with rs.next() and read columns via rs.getString("name"), rs.getInt("age").
Updating: executeUpdate() for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE returns the number of affected rows — check it!
Transactions group operations: setAutoCommit(false), run your statements, then commit() — or rollback() on error, keeping the database consistent.
Resources must be closed in reverse order (ResultSet, Statement, Connection) — try-with-resources handles it; connections are expensive, so pool them in production (HikariCP).
The driver itself is a dependency (e.g., org.postgresql:postgresql or com.h2database:h2) — code to the java.sql interfaces, never to driver internals.
Handle SQLException explicitly: get the SQLState code and vendor message for real diagnostics. Also watch for timeout and connection-loss handling.
Modern alternatives (JPA/Hibernate) sit ON TOP of JDBC — understanding JDBC first makes ORMs comprehensible.
commonMistakes: Concatenating user input into SQL — the #1 security bug in history. Parameters only.
Using Statement instead of PreparedStatement — same injection risk, no plan caching.
Forgetting try-with-resources on Connection/Statement/ResultSet — leaked connections exhaust the pool.
Calling getString on the wrong column name — SQLException at runtime; double-check your SQL's aliases.
Auto-commit on multi-step writes — one failure mid-way leaves partial data; use transactions.

exercises.title: Parameterized lookup
exercises.prompt: Write a method that takes a username string and safely queries a users table with PreparedStatement, printing matching rows.

exercises.title: Transactional transfer
exercises.prompt: Simulate a bank transfer: decrement account A, increment account B, in one transaction with rollback on failure.

title: HTTP Clients: Talking to the Web
analogy: Making an HTTP request is ordering takeout: you pick a restaurant (URL), say what you want (method + body), the kitchen replies with your food and a status — 200 means 'delivered', 404 means 'no such dish'. The java.net.http client is your courier app.
content: HTTP is the web's request/response language: a client sends a request (method, URL, headers, optional body), a server answers with a status code, headers, and a body.

Key methods: GET (fetch), POST (create/send data), PUT (replace), DELETE (remove). Status classes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error (404 not found, 400 bad request), 5xx server error (500).
The modern client (Java 11+): HttpClient.newHttpClient(), HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("...")) with .GET() or .POST(BodyPublishers.ofString(json)), then .send() or .sendAsync().
Synchronous send blocks the calling thread until the response arrives; sendAsync returns a CompletableFuture<HttpResponse> so your app stays responsive.
Read the body with BodyHandlers.ofString() (text), ofByteArray(), or ofLines(). Status lives in response.statusCode() and headers in response.headers().
Set headers with .header("Content-Type", "application/json") or .headers(k, v, k2, v2) for things like auth tokens and Accept.
Timeouts prevent hangs: .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)) on the request builder — network code MUST have timeouts.
Handle failures explicitly: check status codes (2xx expected), catch IOException (network down) and InterruptedException (thread interrupted).
JSON bodies are just strings to HTTP — you serialize/deserialize with a library (next lesson!).
URL (legacy) still works but is clunky; HttpClient is the modern, feature-complete choice (HTTP/2, async, redirects configurable via .followRedirects(NORMAL)).
commonMistakes: No timeout — a dead server hangs your thread forever. Always set .timeout().
Forgetting to check statusCode — a 404 page parses like data and crashes later.
Ignoring IOException/InterruptedException handling — the compiler makes you, and you should.
Using HTTP for sensitive data — HTTPS is non-negotiable for anything real.
Blocking the main thread with sync calls in web apps — use sendAsync there.
