exercises.prompt: Send a GET request to https://httpbin.org/get with a name query parameter and print the status and body length.

exercises.title: Async fetch two APIs
exercises.prompt: Fetch two URLs asynchronously with sendAsync and print both results when both complete (use thenCombine or allOf).

title: JSON: The Web's Data Format
analogy: JSON is like a labeled cardboard box with compartments: objects are boxes with named pockets, arrays are egg cartons (ordered slots), strings/numbers are the contents. Everyone (every language) agrees on the box design, so any two systems can ship data to each other.
content: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format: objects { "key": value }, arrays [v1, v2], values being strings, numbers, booleans, null, or nested structures.
JSON has exactly one syntax — which is why it won: Python, Java, JS, Go all parse the same bytes.
The shape maps beautifully to Java records: {"name":"Ada","age":36} -> record Person(String name, int age).
Real-world JSON usually flows over HTTP (see the HTTP lesson) — parse response bodies into objects, serialize objects into request bodies.
In production, use a library: Jackson (jackson-databind) or Gson — ObjectMapper.readValue(json, Person.class) and writeValueAsString(person) — with annotations like @JsonProperty for renames.
No library needed for tiny jobs: java.text is awkward, but a simple hand-rolled parser is educational and fine for one-off scripts.
Text blocks (Java 15+) make embedding JSON in code readable: String json = """ {"name": "Duke"} """;.
Escaping is the classic gotcha: quotes and backslashes inside strings need \" and \\; forgetting them corrupts the document.
Validate by parsing: a malformed JSON fails loudly (JsonParseException) — never hand-build JSON with string concatenation when you can serialize.
Common traps: trailing commas (illegal), single quotes (illegal — JSON only allows double), comments (illegal — no comments in JSON!).
Numbers: JSON numbers are doubles-ish — big longs and money lose precision; send money as strings when it matters.
commonMistakes: Building JSON with string concatenation and forgetting to escape quotes — one user input with a quote and the document explodes.
Single quotes or unquoted keys — legal in JavaScript, ILLEGAL in JSON.
Trailing commas after the last element — a classic silent parser error.
Assuming numbers survive round-trips — use strings for IDs and money.
Ignoring parse exceptions — a bad response body is a bug to surface, not swallow.

exercises.title: Mini parser
exercises.prompt: Write a function that extracts the value of a named field from a simple flat JSON object string (regex or manual scan).

exercises.title: JSON of a record list
exercises.prompt: Extend the mini serializer to handle a list of Person records (or just print a hand-built one using text blocks).

title: Design Patterns: Proven Blueprints
analogy: Design patterns are like chess openings: you could invent your own from scratch each game, but masters studied what works and named it. Learn the names and shapes, and you can discuss strategy with any developer — and recognize when to use (or NOT use) them.
content: Design patterns are reusable solutions to recurring design problems — not code to copy, but shapes to recognize. The classic catalog: the GoF (Gang of Four) book.
Creational patterns manage object creation: Singleton (one instance), Factory Method (delegate creation to subclasses), Builder (step-by-step construction for complex objects).
Singleton: private constructor + static instance. Use it sparingly (it's global state); Java's enums give you a bulletproof singleton: enum Config { INSTANCE }.
Builder shines for objects with many optional fields — fluent API: new Pizza.Builder().size(LARGE).cheese(true).build(); Records cover most simple cases, but builders win for optional-heavy configs.
Structural patterns shape composition: Adapter (translate one interface to another), Decorator (wrap behavior — think BufferedReader wrapping a Reader).
java.io is a decorator showcase: new BufferedInputStream(new FileInputStream(...)) layers behavior without modifying classes.
Behavioral patterns coordinate behavior: Strategy (swap algorithms — Comparator is the textbook Strategy), Observer (publish/subscribe), Command (encapsulate an action as an object).
The JDK is pattern-paved: streams = Iterator/Visitor vibes, java.util.function.* = Strategy, Executors = Factory, String.valueOf = Factory Method.
The real skill is knowing when NOT to: over-engineering with 10 patterns for a 50-line program is a design smell. Patterns earn their keep in evolving, multi-developer codebases.
Modern Java shrinks the need: records + lambdas + sealed types cover Builder/Strategy/Template territories with plain language features.
commonMistakes: Applying patterns 'because they're famous' — a Singleton that's really just a global variable, a Builder for a two-field object.
Forgetting that patterns solve design problems, not performance problems — measure before 'optimizing' with patterns.
Hand-rolling patterns the JDK already provides — prefer existing abstractions (Comparator, Executors, streams).
Copying pattern code verbatim — adapt the shape, don't paste the implementation.
Using Singleton for mutable shared state across threads — now you have a race condition with global reach.

exercises.prompt: Write a builder for a User class (name required, optional email and phone), and build one with only name + email.

title: Spring: The Enterprise Framework
analogy: Spring is the restaurant manager of your app. Instead of each waiter (class) cooking their own food (building their own dependencies), everyone just calls out what they need, and the manager (the Spring container) brings it to them. Nobody knows who cooked the meal — they just receive it (dependency injection).
content: Spring is the de facto enterprise Java framework: it manages your objects' lifecycle and wiring via Inversion of Control (IoC) — a container creates and connects your beans.
Dependency Injection (DI) is the core idea: a class receives its dependencies (constructor parameters) instead of creating them (new ... inside the class).
Benefits: loose coupling (swap implementations without touching callers), easy testing (inject mocks), and configuration lives in one place.
In Spring, @Component (or the specialized @Service, @Repository, @Controller) marks a class as a bean — Spring instantiates it and adds it to the application context.
@Autowired (or constructor injection via a Lombok @RequiredArgsConstructor) asks Spring to provide the dependency — constructor injection is the recommended style.
The application context is the container: ApplicationContext ctx = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class); ctx.getBean(...) is how you reach a bean manually.
Spring Boot builds on Spring: it auto-configures servers (embedded Tomcat), starters bundle common dependencies, and @SpringBootApplication + main() launches a whole web app.
Beans are singletons by default — safe when stateless (which they should be). @Scope("prototype") opts out.
Spring's magic is reflection + annotations in action: it scans for @Component, reads @Autowired, and wires via constructor/method injection.
A hand-rolled mini container (see code) shows the essence: a map of name -> supplier, with dependencies pulled from the map.
Real Spring apps: @RestController + @GetMapping for APIs, @Service for business logic, @Repository for data access — layered, testable, DI-wired.
commonMistakes: Field injection (@Autowired on fields) — hard to test and hides dependencies; prefer constructor injection.
Making beans stateful — singletons shared across requests must be stateless (no mutable instance fields).
Creating dependencies with new inside a bean — defeats DI; let the container wire them.
Forgetting @Component on a class then wondering why autowiring fails — the container only knows registered classes.
Jumping to Spring Boot before understanding DI — the annotation magic looks like magic only without the mental model from this lesson.

exercises.prompt: Write the same feature twice: once with a class creating its dependency via new, once receiving it via constructor. Compare and explain.

title: Unit Testing with JUnit
analogy: A unit test is a contract with your future self: every time the code changes, the test asks 'does it still do what it promised?' Like a quality inspector on an assembly line, it checks every product without being asked — automatically, on every build.
content: Unit tests verify one unit (usually a method/class) in isolation — fast, deterministic, and run on every build so regressions surface immediately.
The structure: Arrange (set up inputs), Act (call the method), Assert (check the result) — also known as given/when/then.
JUnit 5 (org.junit.jupiter) is the standard: @Test methods, assertions like assertEquals, assertTrue, assertNotNull, and assertThrows for exceptions.
Use @BeforeEach for common setup (runs before each test) and @AfterEach for teardown — keeps tests independent and repeatable.
Test boundaries and edge cases, not just happy paths: empty inputs, nulls, zero, max values, invalid data — bugs live at the edges.
Test the exception: assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> service.setAge(-1)) checks both the exception type and the trigger.
Name tests as behavior: shouldThrowWhenAgeNegative, not test1. A good name reads like a spec sentence.
Tests run in any order and must be isolated — shared mutable state between tests is the #1 flakiness cause.
Test doubles replace real dependencies: mocks (Mockito) assert behavior; stubs return canned data. Fakes are small in-memory implementations.
TDD (Test-Driven Development): red (write failing test), green (make it pass), refactor (clean up) — the loop that produces designed, tested code.
Run them with the build tool: mvn test or gradle test — the gate before merge keeps teams honest.
A tiny hand-rolled test runner (see code) demos the concept; JUnit does this professionally with reporting.
commonMistakes: Testing implementation details instead of behavior — tests that break on refactors are chained to the code.
Only testing the happy path — the bug is waiting in the edge cases.
Tests that depend on order, time, or shared state — flaky by design.
Asserting with print statements instead of assertions — a green run must mean 'verified', not 'looks right'.
One test asserting ten things — split them; a failing test should tell you exactly which behavior broke.

exercises.prompt: Write a reverse(String) method and tests for: normal word, empty string, single char, null handling.

exercises.prompt: Write a method that converts 0-99 to words (e.g., 42 -> "forty-two") and test boundary values: 0, 10, 13, 20, 42, 99.

title: SOLID Principles
tagline: Five rules for code that survives
analogy: SOLID is the building code of software architecture: each rule is a structural guideline that prevents a specific collapse. Follow the code, and your building (codebase) can grow new floors (features) without tearing down walls (rewrites).
content: SOLID is five design principles that keep code maintainable as it grows: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, Dependency Inversion.
S — Single Responsibility: a class should have one reason to change. A class that parses, stores, AND renders data changes for three different reasons.
Signs of violation: god classes (does everything), shotgun surgery (one change touches many classes), methods longer than a screen.
O — Open/Closed: open for extension, closed for modification. Add behavior with new classes (strategy/interface implementations), not by editing existing logic.
L — Liskov Substitution: a subclass must be usable anywhere its parent is. Classic violation: a Square extending Rectangle breaks setWidth()/setHeight() invariants — prefer composition.
The LSP test: if code using the parent breaks with the child, the hierarchy is wrong. (Is-a in words is not is-a in behavior.)
I — Interface Segregation: no client should depend on methods it doesn't use. Fat interfaces force stub implementations; split into small role interfaces.
D — Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions, not concretions. High-level logic should reference interfaces; the concrete choice lives at the composition root (main / DI container).
DI in action: a ReportPrinter taking OutputTarget (console/file/network) is SOLID-D; taking PrintStream is more practical — principles guide, they don't dictate.
SOLID interacts with tests: SOLID code is easy to test because dependencies are injectable and responsibilities are small.
Start pragmatic: SRP and D on day one; reach for the rest as the codebase actually grows.
commonMistakes: Applying SRP as 'one method per class' — it's about reasons to change, not size.
Breaking LSP with inheritance shortcuts — Square extends Rectangle is the classic; compose instead.
Interface with 10 methods used partially — split it; clients pay for what they use (ISP).
Depending on concrete classes at every layer — DI them at the top.
Treating SOLID as a checklist to score 100% — it's a compass, applied where it pays.

exercises.prompt: Write a Greeter that depends on a GreetingFormatter interface, with English and Spanish implementations — swap at runtime.

title: Clean Code in Java
analogy: Clean code is a well-written recipe: ingredients measured, steps numbered, notes in the margins. Messy code is a napkin scrawled during a rush — it cooks today but nobody (including future-you) can follow it tomorrow. Code is read 10x more than it's written.
content: The #1 rule: code is for humans. The compiler accepts anything; your teammates (and future you) have to understand it.
Names: intention-revealing. daysSinceLastLogin beats d; isActive beats flag. Names should answer 'why it exists, what it does, how it's used'.
Small methods: a method should do one thing at one level of abstraction. extractServiceCall or handleTimeout as method names guide readers.
Avoid magic numbers: MAX_RETRIES = 3 is self-documenting; 3 in a loop body means nothing. Prefer enums/constants.
Comments: say WHY, not what. What the code does should be readable from the code itself; a comment explaining a strange business rule or a tricky invariant is gold.
Formatting: let the IDE formatter own it (one style, no debates). Consistent indentation and blank-line grouping cost nothing and pay constantly.
Avoid null returns: return Optional.empty() or an empty collection — callers forget null checks; empty collections never NPE.
Use records for data carriers, var for obvious types (var names = new ArrayList<String>() reads better typed).
Fail fast and loudly: validate inputs at the boundary, use custom exceptions with context, never swallow errors.
The Boy Scout rule: leave the code cleaner than you found it — small refactors on every touch prevent decay.
Code review mindset: read your own diff before pushing; if you have to think twice, extract it.
commonMistakes: Saving keystrokes with cryptic names (x, d, t) — clarity is free with autocomplete.
Writing comments that repeat the code ('// adds 1 to x') instead of explaining the why.
Giant methods with nested ifs — extract; a method over ~20 lines is a candidate.
Returning null when an empty collection/Optional says the same thing safely.
Leaving dead code and commented-out blocks — the git history keeps it; delete it.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite a method that uses magic numbers (100, 0.05, 18) with named constants and explain each.

title: Performance Tuning
analogy: Performance work is like dieting: weighing yourself first (profiling) tells you where the fat actually is. Optimizing blind is dieting by guessing which meal is fattening — you'll cut salads and keep the butter. Measure, then act.
content: Rule zero: measure before optimizing. The profiler is the scale — guessing which code is slow is usually wrong. Tools: IDE profilers, jcmd/jstat, async-profiler, JFR (JDK Flight Recorder).
Complexity first: O(n^2) beats any constant-factor trick. A HashMap lookup beats a linear scan the moment n grows — algorithmic wins dwarf micro-optimizations.
The 90/10 rule: ~90% of time is usually in ~10% of code. Optimize hot paths, leave the rest clean.
Strings: use StringBuilder (or String.join) for loops concatenating many strings — each + in a loop allocates a new String.
Boxing: in hot loops, prefer primitives and IntStream; Integer boxing/unboxing allocates objects and pressure the GC.
Collections: ArrayList over LinkedList for index access; HashMap over TreeMap for lookups; EnumMap when possible; sized initial capacity (new ArrayList<>(1_000)) avoids resizing.
Memory leaks are silent slowdowns: static collections growing forever, listeners never removed, caches without eviction — GC churn climbs until OOM.
Streams vs loops: streams add little overhead; pick for clarity. In ultra-hot paths (billions of iterations), a loop wins; in real apps, it rarely matters.
I/O is the true bottleneck: buffer it (BufferedReader), batch network calls, avoid per-row DB queries in loops.
Premature optimization is the root of evil (Knuth): write clean code, profile, optimize only measured hotspots, and re-measure after each change.
JMH (Java Microbenchmark Harness) is the proper way to benchmark micro-ops — hand-timed loops get JIT-warmed and lie to you.
commonMistakes: Optimizing before measuring — you'll polish code that runs 0.1% of the time.
Benchmarking without JVM warmup — the JIT makes the first runs slower; results mislead.
Replacing clear code with clever code for a 2% gain in non-hot paths.
Forgetting algorithmic complexity — an O(n^2) with fast constants still loses at scale.
Ignoring memory: allocation volume (boxing, strings) often matters more than CPU ops — watch GC logs.

title: Debugging Like a Pro
analogy: Debugging is detective work: the stack trace is your crime scene, the debugger is your magnifying glass, and the bug is a suspect with an alibi that doesn't hold. Professionals don't guess — they gather evidence, form a theory, and test it in small steps.
content: Start with the message: read the full stack trace top-down. The top frame is where it blew up; then find the FIRST frame that's in YOUR code — that's usually the real culprit.
The exception tells you what went wrong; the stack tells you where. Combine both before touching anything.
NullPointerException hunting: find the first line in your code, look at every '.' on that line — one of those references is null. Check with a quick print or debugger.
Reproduce first: a bug you can't reproduce can't be fixed. Capture the exact input, environment, and steps.
Debuggers beat println: set breakpoints, step over/into, inspect variables and stack. Every serious IDE (IntelliJ, VS Code) has one — learn its three step buttons.
Binary search the bug: comment out halves of the code to locate the failing region — bisecting is dramatically faster than reading line by line.
The rubber duck: explain your code line-by-line to an inanimate object. Saying the wrong assumption out loud finds the bug shockingly often.

Print what you believe: log the inputs at the start of a suspect method and the outputs at the end — theory, not noise. System.out is fine for small scripts; use a logger (System.Logger, slf4j) in real apps.
Check assumptions about types: 'it's a String... oh wait, it's Integer'. Var/IDE inspection makes this visible.
Fix ONE thing at a time and re-test — multi-fix debugging produces multi-bugs.
When stuck: take a break, re-read the error verbatim, or simplify — a minimal repro (10-line snippet) is the professional's secret weapon.
commonMistakes: Reading only the exception type and not the trace — the where is usually the more valuable half.
Fixing the symptom (adding a null check at the crash site) instead of the cause (who passed null).
println everywhere then deleting them all — use the debugger, it's faster.
Changing three things between runs — you can't tell which fixed it.
Not reproducing with minimal input — 500-line repros hide what a 5-line one reveals.

title: Modern Java: What's New
tagline: From Java 8 to 21 in one lesson
analogy: Java 8 is like a smartphone from 2014: works fine, but the modern model (Java 17/21) has better cameras (records), better keyboards (switch expressions), and battery life (performance). Learning the new features isn't just novelty — each one removes whole classes of boilerplate and bugs.
content: Java 8 (2014) was the big bang: lambdas, streams, Optional, and the new date/time API — it changed how Java code looks forever.
Java 10: var for local variables — List<String> names = new ArrayList<>() becomes var names = new ArrayList<String>()... type is inferred; use when the type is obvious.
Java 11: HTTP client (java.net.http), toList() on streams (well, 16), string methods isBlank, strip, lines, repeat.
Java 14: switch expressions — int days = switch (month) { case JAN, MAR -> 31; ... default -> 0; } with no break/fall-through and arrow syntax.
Java 14/15: text blocks — """ multi-line strings """ end HTML/JSON/SQL embedding battles with escaping.
Java 15/16: records (data carriers, this course has a whole lesson) and pattern matching for instanceof: if (obj instanceof Point p) — no cast.
Java 16: sealed classes — hierarchy under your control: sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square — exhaustive switch guarantees safety.
Java 17 (LTS): the default choice for new projects — pattern matching for switch in preview then final (21), sealed finalized, records finalized.
Java 21 (LTS): virtual threads (millions of threads for I/O-heavy apps — threads became cheap), pattern matching for switch finalized, sequenced collections.
Choosing a version: prefer LTS (17 or 21) for production; tools like Gradle/Maven plugins and your IDE set the floor. Upgrading 17 -> 21 is usually painless.
The feature cadence changed: 6-month releases with LTS every 2 years — you don't have to chase every release, just the LTSs.
commonMistakes: Staying on Java 8 out of habit — LTS 17/21 are mature, faster, and free to upgrade for most codebases.
Using var where the type matters for clarity (var result = someService.doStuff() hides what it returns).
Old-style switch with fall-through when switch expressions exist — arrow syntax is shorter and safer.
Manually writing equals/hashCode/getters for data classes when records do it in one line.
Hand-casting with instanceof before using pattern matching — verbosity with zero benefit.

title: Interview Prep: Ace the Java Interview
analogy: An interview is a flight simulator: the tasks are realistic but safe, and the examiner watches how you think, not just whether you land. Prepare the checklists (core topics), practice the takeoffs (coding), and remember the goal is showing your process — not memorized answers.
content: The interview map: OOP (inheritance vs composition, interfaces vs abstract classes), collections (when which), strings (pool, immutability), exceptions, concurrency, JVM basics, SQL basics, and one or two system-design-lite questions.

Classic #1 — 'Difference between abstract class and interface?': abstract = shared state + behavior skeleton (single inheritance); interface = contract, multiple implementation, default methods since 8, records/sealed interplay. Mention both can have default/static methods.

Classic #2 — 'What is the String pool and immutability?': literals live in the pool (shared, GC'd on demand), String is immutable (security, hashing, thread-safety), StringBuilder for mutation, == vs equals trap.

Classic #3 — 'equals() vs hashCode() contract': equal objects MUST have equal hash codes; contract broken = HashSet/HashMap breakage. Give the override recipe: Objects.hash for hashCode, instanceof-based equals.
Classic #4 — 'What happens if a HashMap key is mutable and changed?': the entry is lost in its old bucket — don't mutate keys; use records/immutable keys.
Coding problems: clarify requirements FIRST (ask about edge cases, inputs, constraints), then state your approach out loud, then code, then test with examples.
Think out loud: interviewers grade reasoning. Say 'I'll use a HashMap for O(1) lookups' and 'I'm checking the empty case' — narration is points.
Common coding topics: two pointers, sliding window, frequency maps, stack for nesting problems, sorting + binary search — practice these patterns.
Behavioral (STAR): Situation, Task, Action, Result — 2-minute stories of real wins, with numbers when possible.
Trap questions: 'What's your biggest weakness?' (pick a real one + mitigation), 'Do you have questions for us?' (ALWAYS yes — ask about team, codebase, growth).
Whiteboard style: write clean, compilable-in-your-head Java — name variables well, handle the trivial cases, keep methods small.
Your moat: this course's capstone + challenges + quizzes = real evidence of depth. Bring the projects you built.
commonMistakes: Memorizing answers without understanding — one follow-up question exposes it; drill the why.
Diving into code before clarifying the problem — ask about inputs, sizes, and edge cases first.
Silent coding — the interviewer can't grade what they can't hear; narrate your plan.
Forgetting to test your own code — run the example through mentally, check empty/single/large cases.
Not preparing questions to ask — 'do you have questions?' is a real filter, not small talk.

title: Capstone: Build a Real App
tagline: Put it all together — and ship it
analogy: Every lesson so far was a musical scale. Now you compose a song: a real, useful program with a UI, persistence, and edge cases. The difference between a course-grader and an engineer is shipping something end-to-end — you're about to.
content: The project: an Expense Tracker CLI — add expenses (date, category, amount, note), list them, filter by category, show totals and monthly summaries, and save/load to a file.
Phase 1 — Domain: record Expense(LocalDate date, String category, double amount, String note). Records = immutable data, free equals/toString.
Phase 2 — Storage: save expenses to expenses.json or a simple text format with Files.readString/writeString; load on startup; handle missing file gracefully.
Phase 3 — Logic: totals by category (Collectors.groupingBy + summing), monthly summaries (groupingBy(Expense::getMonth)), top categories — your streams lesson pays off here.
Phase 4 — Interface: a tiny REPL (read-eval-print loop): prompt with a Scanner, commands add / list / total / filter / quit, clear error messages.
Phase 5 — Robustness: catch NumberFormatException on bad amounts, IllegalArgumentException on negative values, IOException on save failures — with useful messages, never crashes.
Architecture discipline: one class per concern — ExpenseStore (I/O), ExpenseStats (aggregations), CliApp (I/O loop). Testable and clean.
Testing mindset: write a small main-based smoke test or use the mini test runner pattern to verify stats math before wiring the CLI.
Extension menu (pick one): JSON format with your mini serializer, a REST fetch of currency rates (HttpClient lesson), a simple Swing/GUI or web UI, sorting views.
The definition of done: runs anywhere with java, survives restarts (data persisted), handles bad input, has at least 3 commands, and the code would pass your own review.
Then: refactor pass (clean code lesson), a README, and show it off — your capstone is interview gold.
commonMistakes: Skipping the storage layer and testing only in-memory — persistence is where real apps live or die.
One giant main() with everything — the 'god method' that's untestable and unreviewable.
No error handling on user input — one bad number crashes the whole app.
Fancy features before the basics work — finish add/list/total first, extend after.
Not saving data — if a restart loses everything, it's a demo, not an app.
